title: From DNA damage to systemic immunity: Interaction networks in radio-immunotherapy

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《From DNA damage to systemic immunity: Interaction networks in radio-immunotherapy》：研究问题的原文依据。

【How radiotherapy potentiates immunotherapy · p0205】The strongest evidence concerns checkpoint blockade, and it is mechanistically specific rather than merely additive. Twyman-Saint Victor et al. showed that radiation, CTLA-4 blockade and PD-L1 blockade act through non-redundant mechanisms in melanoma: CTLA-4 blockade depletes regulatory T cells and raises the ratio of CD8-positive T cells to regulatory T cells, radiation diversifies the intratumoral T cell receptor repertoire, and PD-L1 blockade reverses the T cell exhaustion that limits both (Twyman-Saint Victor et al., 2015). Stereotactic irradiation increases cross-presentation of tumor antigen and expands antigen-specific T cells, an effect amplified by PD-1 blockade (Sharabi et al., 2015), and the clonotypes expanded by radiation combined with CTLA-4 blockade differ from those expanded by either treatment alone. In patients, adding radiotherapy to CTLA-4 blockade produced objective responses in chemorefractory metastatic lung cancer, with induction of IFN-β and expansion of T cell clones as immunological correlates (Formenti et al., 2018). Durvalumab consolidation after concurrent chemoradiotherapy is an established strategy for unresectable stage III NSCLC (Hui et al., 2019), and a pooled analysis of two trials suggested higher response rates and improved survival with radiotherapy plus pembrolizumab, including a signal in PD-L1-negative disease; this subgroup finding and its proposed antigen-release mechanism remain hypothesis-generating (Theelen et al., 2021).

【Nanotechnology-enabled delivery · p0290】Radiotherapy remains a standard component of treatment for many cancers, particularly in localized or locoregionally advanced disease, and the emergence of immunotherapy has introduced new possibilities for enhancing radiotherapy outcomes. However, despite its promise, immunotherapy still carries the risk of off-target effects, even if at a lower rate. Improving immunotherapy effectiveness is complex and depends on multiple factors, including cancer antigen expression, antigen presentation, and the activation, transport, and infiltration of immune cells to the tumor site. In addition to established and investigational immunotherapy approaches, nanotechnology-based delivery platforms are being investigated as strategies to enhance antitumor immune responses. Nanomaterials are being developed to improve the delivery, pharmacokinetics or tumor localization of selected immunotherapeutic agents, although consistent clinical outcome benefits remain to be established for many platforms. However, as an emerging technology, the safety of nanomaterials in human health must be carefully considered. Some nanomaterials are difficult to degrade within the body, and long-term exposure may lead to accumulation and potential safety risks. Additionally, the molecular interactions between nanomaterials and immunotherapy require further investigation to understand their impact fully. Future nanotechnology-mediated immunotherapy should prioritise safety assessments and potential side effects to ensure its viability as a clinical treatment option.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《From DNA damage to systemic immunity: Interaction networks in radio-immunotherapy》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Biomarkers and patient selection · p0285】A practical biomarker strategy for combined radiotherapy and immunotherapy has to answer two different questions, and most current candidates answer only one of them. The first question is whether the tumor can generate an immune response after irradiation. It is addressed by tumor-intrinsic markers, including PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden and mismatch repair status, and, more specifically for this setting, by the integrity of cGAS–STING pathway components, whose loss or epigenetic suppression in some tumor types may impair radiation-induced type I interferon signaling, although predictive value remains to be clinically validated. The second question is whether the patient retains an effector compartment capable of executing that response. It is addressed by host and dynamic markers, including the absolute lymphocyte count and its nadir during treatment, the estimated dose to circulating blood, the T cell receptor repertoire measured before and after irradiation, and circulating tumor DNA or exosomal double-stranded DNA as a non-invasive proxy for the interferogenic DNA released from the irradiated field. Radiomic estimates of CD8 infiltration may enable non-invasive assessment across multiple lesions when imaging quality and model domain are appropriate, but require external validation and lesion-level calibration (Huang et al., 2024).

【A mechanism-based framework for combination design · p0235】The strategies described above can be organized by the mechanistic role that the partner agent plays relative to radiation, and four classes cover most of the current landscape. Innate immune agonists supply or amplify the sensing step, and they are appropriate when the tumor cannot generate an interferon response by itself. Adaptive immune enhancers act on the effector pool, and they are appropriate when priming occurs but is not sustained. Microenvironment remodeling agents remove suppressive constraints imposed by regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells or TGF-β, and they are appropriate when effector cells are present but non-functional. Delivery and targeting technologies change where the signal is generated rather than what the signal is.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《From DNA damage to systemic immunity: Interaction networks in radio-immunotherapy》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Dose dependence of the radiation-immune response: low-dose radiation as an illustrative case · p0035】The term RadScopal effect is often applied loosely to any immunomodulatory action of low-dose radiation. We use it here only in the narrower sense intended by its originators, that is, as the name of a specific triple-combination strategy, and we describe the general immunomodulatory actions of low-dose radiation without that label. A number of studies have reported immunomodulatory effects of low-dose radiation. The concept of the RadScopal effect was coined by Welsh and colleagues to describe a strategy that combines low-dose and high-dose radiotherapy to different lesions (Barsoumian et al., 2020). It is a combining triple therapy approach (high-dose radiotherapy + low-dose radiotherapy + immunotherapy), in which high-dose radiotherapy directs at primary tumors, low-dose radiotherapy deliver to secondary tumors. Through their investigation, they combined high-dose radiation to “prime” T cells at the primary cancer site, with low-dose radiation targeted to metastatic cancers to “modulate the stroma”. This strategy showed the low-dose radiation has benefits to reprogram the cancer environment and improve the infiltration and function of effector immune cells into secondary cancers (Barsoumian et al., 2020). Zhou et al. conducted a prospective phase I study. Patients received stereotactic body radiotherapy of 30 Gy for small lesions and low-dose radiation of 2 Gy for large lesion concurrently followed by PD-1 inhibitor. The regimen was feasible and yielded a median progression-free survival of 8.6 months; efficacy and any association with PD-1/PD-L1 status require validation in controlled trials using prespecified assays and thresholds (Zhou et al., 2023). The RadScopal rationale is that high-dose irradiation of selected lesions may provide antigenic priming, whereas low-dose irradiation of other lesions may, in some settings, remodel suppressive stroma and improve immune-cell trafficking; both components can have immunostimulatory or suppressive effects depending on context. Thus, low-dose radiation serves as a potential tool to improve the immunogenicity of radiotherapy, and it has also been reported to remodel the tumor immune microenvironment and enhance the effect of anti-CTLA-4 therapy (Dong et al., 2025). Further research is needed to understand fully its therapeutic potential.

【Radiation and systemic immunity: humoral and lymphocyte-subset evidence · p0045】Humoral immunity mainly produces antibodies via B lymphocytes to combat extracellular pathogens and the toxins produced. Because these antibodies are present in bodily fluids, including blood, lymphatic fluid and tissue fluid, this arm of immunity is termed humoral immunity. The major cellular and molecular components of humoral immunity include B cells and plasma cells that produce immunoglobulins, with helper T cells and antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells (DCs) and macrophages providing antigen presentation and regulatory signals. The function of humoral immunity defend against extracellular threats such as pathogens and toxins, generating immune memory to achieve long-term immunity through B cells, and providing systemic protection by antibodies’ circulation throughout the body with the blood. The study of effects of low-dose radiation on humoral immunity has various results. The results of low-dose radiation role in early study on occupational workers were inhibition function whereas recent reports are stimulating effects. An early study among residents of territories contaminated with radionuclides after Chernobyl accident showed low-dose radiation exposure led to a decrease in the counts of large granular lymphocytes (Asfandiiarova et al., 1998). Another study showed a 0.1 Gy dose of radiation had an immunosuppressing effect through the inactivation of helper cells in the early period of a postnatal ontogeny (Sharetskii & Abramova, 2006). Bogdándi et al. found that low doses altered splenocyte subset responses and decreased Th1- and Th2-type cytokine expression, whereas B cells were relatively resistant at low doses but became among the most sensitive subsets after 2 Gy exposure (Bogdándi et al., 2010). Gyuleva et al. assessed humoral immune parameters among nuclear power plant workers with the low-dose radiation exposure within the range of 0.06 to 766.36 mSv and found while less than 100 mSv low prevalence of Th1 immune response but Th2 response occurred at doses beyond 100 mSv (Gyuleva et al., 2015). A study among interventional cardiologists showed a significant increase in the expression of the activation marker CD69 on stimulated CD4+ T cells, together with altered serum immunoglobulin G levels (Zakeri et al., 2010). Schoenfeld et al. performed a phase II trial in patients with metastatic NSCLC, in that patients received durvalumab (anti-PD-L1) plus tremelimumab (anti-CTLA-4) immunotherapy alone or with low-dose (0.5 Gy) or hypofractionated radiotherapy (24 Gy). They found no difference within immunoradiotherapy alone and low-dose radiation group and no survival improvement. They speculated that lymphocyte death may have blunted the favorable immunological function of radiotherapy (Schoenfeld et al., 2022). Taken together, these humoral data are less consistent than the cellular data, and they are best interpreted as evidence that B cell and antibody compartments are sensitive to dose, to species and to the timing of sampling, rather than as evidence of a uniform stimulatory effect.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《From DNA damage to systemic immunity: Interaction networks in radio-immunotherapy》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Fig. 1 · fig1】Fig. 1 Classification of molecular interactions and an integrative mechanism of radiotherapy-immunotherapy synergy. A detailed and holistic conceptual framework for understanding radiotherapy-immunotherapy synergy. Panel (A) establishes a structured taxonomy of the primary molecular interaction types, including protein–protein, protein–DNA, and gene–drug interactions, to define the relevant molecular dictionary. Panel (B) presents an evidence-based, integrative mechanistic flowchart detailing the dynamic interplay from local radiotherapy to systemic, distant tumor response. It illustrates the critical transition from a suppressive to an inflamed microenvironment, specifically highlighting how PD-1/PD-L1 blockade occludes checkpoint signaling. This may enhance antigen presentation and T-cell priming, thereby increasing the likelihood of systemic antitumor immune responses, including occasional abscopal responses and distant tumor regression in selected contexts. RT, radiotherapy.

【Fig. 2 · fig2】Fig. 2 Radiotherapy-mediated reprogramming of the tumor immune microenvironment. (A) Comparative overview of immunologically cold vs hot tumor phenotypes, illustrating the role of radiotherapy in converting cold tumors to hot states and potentially improving immunotherapy outcomes. (B) A detailed molecular mechanistic flowchart showing how radiotherapy-induced cellular damage activates the cGAS–STING, NF-κB, and JAK–STAT pathways. Each pathway’s cascade and associated molecular brakes are depicted. The convergence of these signals determines the transition to either an immune-activated “hot” tumor responsive to ICB or an immunosuppressive tumor with primary or acquired resistance. RT, radiotherapy.

【Fig. 3 · fig3】Fig. 3 Dose- and time-dependent immune-inflammatory dynamics after irradiation. This matrix details the spatiotemporal evolution of immune responses across three radiation regimens: high-dose/hypofractionated, conventional, and low-dose. It traces the biological cascade from initial DNA damage (minutes) to long-term immune remodeling (weeks/months). Preclinical studies suggest that sufficiently high single-fraction doses can induce TREX1 in a dose- and context-dependent manner, promoting cytosolic DNA degradation and potentially attenuating cGAS–STING-dependent immunogenicity; the clinical threshold and consequences remain context dependent.
